meta.trial_name: AURORA (A Study to Evaluate the Use of Rosuvastatin in Subjects on Regular Hemodialysis: an Assessment of Survival and Cardiovascular Events)
meta.drug: rosuvastatin 10 mg once daily (CRESTOR) vs placebo
meta.mechanism: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin); lowered LDL-C ~43% at 3 months (about 1.1 mmol/L from a baseline of 2.6 mmol/L)
meta.indication: prevention of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI and nonfatal stroke in patients aged 50-80 with end-stage renal disease on maintenance hemodialysis, irrespective of lipid levels

n_randomized.quote: During the recruitment period, from January 2003 through December 2004, a total of 3021 patients were screened, and 2776 patients were randomly assigned to double-blind treatment with rosuvastatin at a dose of 10 mg (1391 patients) or placebo (1385 patients)
n_randomized.note: Intention-to-treat population 2773: 'Of those enrolled, 3 patients were randomly assigned incorrectly and were not included in the intention-to-treat population, leaving a total of 2773 patients.' Registry S3: enrollment 2776 ACTUAL; outcome denominators 1389 vs 1384. Baseline paper S5 (2007) reported 2775 randomized.

median_followup.quote: During a median follow-up period of 3.8 years, 396 patients in the rosuvastatin group and 408 patients in the placebo group reached the primary end point
median_followup.note: Mean follow-up 3.2 years (maximum 5.6) per Results: 'The mean length of follow-up was 3.2 years (maximum, 5.6).' Mean exposure to study drug 2.4 years (median 2.2).

primary_endpoint.value: Time to first major cardiovascular event: nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or death from cardiovascular causes (adjudicated, blinded endpoint committee)
primary_endpoint.quote: The primary end point was the time to a major cardiovascular event, defined as a nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or death from cardiovascular causes.
primary_endpoint.note: Unchanged from design paper S4 and registry S3. Coronary revascularisation was a secondary endpoint, not part of the primary composite (S7 SHARP Discussion stresses this).

inclusion_key_criteria.value: Age 50-80; end-stage renal disease on regular hemodialysis or hemofiltration for >=3 months; no statin in previous 6 months; no expected kidney transplant within 1 year; no life-limiting non-renal disease; irrespective of lipid levels
inclusion_key_criteria.quote: Men and women 50 to 80 years of age who had end-stage renal disease and had been treated with regular hemodialysis or hemofiltration for at least 3 months were recruited from 280 centers in 25 countries. The major exclusion criteria were statin therapy within the previous 6 months, expected kidney transplantation within 1 year, and serious hematologic, neoplastic, gastrointestinal, infectious, or metabolic disease (excluding diabetes) that was predicted to limit life expectancy to less than 1 year.
inclusion_key_criteria.note: Lipid-independent entry per design paper S4: 'More than 2,750 ESRD patients ... have been randomised (1:1), irrespective of baseline lipid levels'. Baseline S5: 26% diabetes, 51% documented CVD or CVD risk equivalent.

planned_events.quote: In the revised calculation of power, we assumed a neutral (0%) treatment effect on stroke 14 and predicted a 19.5% reduction in the rate of major cardiovascular events with active therapy. With a two-sided significance level of 0.05 and 87% power, we estimated that 805 major cardiovascular events were required for analysis.
planned_events.note: Original plan 620 events (S1: 'It was estimated that 620 events would be required for the analysis, assuming a 25% benefit of intervention, 90% power, and a two-sided significance level of 0.05.'; design paper S4: 'The study will continue until 620 subjects have experienced a major cardiovascular event.'). Revised after 4D (2005). Observed 804 events, i.e. the revised target was reached.

With a two-sided significance level of 0.05 and 87% power, we estimated that 805 major cardiovascular events were required for analysis.
assumed_rrr.note: Revised assumption with 0% effect on stroke. Original: 25% reduction with 11%/year placebo event rate (S4: 'it is anticipated that the cardiovascular event rate in the placebo group will be 11% per year').

baseline.quote: After 3 months, the mean reduction in low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels was 43% in patients receiving rosuvastatin, from a mean baseline level of 100 mg per deciliter (2.6 mmol per liter).
baseline.note: Baseline paper S5 (pre-readout, 2007): 'Mean TC and LDL-C levels were 4.53 mmol/l (175 mg/ dl) and 2.57 mmol/l (99 mg/dl), respectively.' Table 1 of S1 (image) not read.

baseline.quote: mean HDL-C and TG levels were 1.16 mmol/l (45 mg/dl) and 1.75 mmol/l (155 mg/dl), respectively.
baseline.note: Read via WebFetch of the PMC page (quote extracted by the fetch tool). Preliminary baseline data on 2775 randomized.

baseline.quote: mean HDL-C and TG levels were 1.16 mmol/l (45 mg/dl) and 1.75 mmol/l (155 mg/dl), respectively.
Mean TC and LDL-C levels were 4.53 mmol/l (175 mg/ dl) and 2.57 mmol/l (99 mg/dl), respectively.

baseline.note: Table row as returned by WebFetch of the PMC page.
NOT FOUND as a reported value (TC 4.53 minus HDL-C 1.16 = 3.37 mmol/L is a derived difference of means).

baseline.note: Wording is ambiguous ('elevated ... by 5.0 mg per liter'); Table 1 (image) not read. Treat as approximate.

baseline.quote: Mean systolic and diastolic blood pressure was 137 and 76 mm Hg, respectively

biomarker_effects.method: central laboratory; percent change from baseline by arm
biomarker_effects.quote: At 3 months, the LDL cholesterol level in the rosuvastatin group was 42.9% lower than the baseline level (mean [±SD] difference, 42±30 mg per deciliter [1.1±0.8 mmol per liter]), as compared with a 1.9% reduction in the placebo group (mean difference, 1.9±23 mg per deciliter [0.05±0.59 mmol per liter]; P<0.001 for the between-group comparison)
biomarker_effects.location: Results, Lipid and C-Reactive Protein Levels; Figure 1A
biomarker_effects.note: Placebo-adjusted values are DERIVED: -42.9% minus -1.9% = -41 percentage points; -1.1 minus -0.05 = -1.05 mmol/L (-42 vs -1.9 mg/dL = about -40 mg/dL). Abstract quotes the within-arm 43%. The difference shrank later: 'Toward the end of the study, there was a trend toward a convergence of the lipid levels in the active-treatment and placebo groups, probably reflecting withdrawals from active therapy and “drop-in” therapy with statins in the placebo group.' Average LDL-C difference over follow-up NOT FOUND (Figure 1A not read).

biomarker_effects.quote: At 3 months, rosuvastatin also reduced the total cholesterol level, by 26.6% (by 47±35 mg per deciliter [1.2±0.9 mmol per liter]), as compared with a 0.5% reduction (1±27 mg per deciliter [0.03±0.70 mmol per liter]) in the placebo group (P<0.001)

the triglyceride level was reduced by 16.2% (by 26±71 mg per deciliter [0.29±0.80 mmol per liter]), as compared with an increase of 0.9% (1.8±72 mg per deciliter [0.02±0.81 mmol per liter]) in the placebo group (P<0.001)

There was a modest increase of 2.9% in the high-density lipoprotein cholesterol level (1.2±10 mg per deciliter [0.03±0.26 mmol per liter]), as compared with an increase of 0.8% (0.4±9.3 mg per deciliter [0.01±0.24 mmol per liter]) in the placebo group (P=0.045)

biomarker_effects.method: median, central laboratory; two-sample sign test
biomarker_effects.quote: The median high-sensitivity C-reactive protein level was elevated at baseline ( Table 1 ) and decreased by 11.5% in the rosuvastatin group at 3 months (by 0.65 mg per liter, vs. an increase of 0.21 mg per liter in the placebo group; P<0.001)

biomarker_effects.note: NOT FOUND: apoB was a tertiary endpoint in design paper S4 but on-treatment apoB is not reported in the S1 text read.

biomarker_effects.timepoint: starting dose 10 mg (earlier rosuvastatin trials, not dialysis patients)
biomarker_effects.method: as cited in the design paper (ref 25, Blasetto et al., rosuvastatin vs other statins)
biomarker_effects.quote: Rosuvastatin is the most efficacious of the available statins for lowering LDL-C levels, causing reductions of 47% at the initial starting dose of 10 mg [25].
biomarker_effects.note: Secondary citation inside the 2005 design paper (pre-readout); the cited trial (ref 25) was not read and the population was not on dialysis. No dialysis-specific phase 2 lipid study of rosuvastatin found. Related pre-readout evidence: 4D (S12) atorvastatin 20 mg lowered median LDL-C 42% (vs 1.3% placebo) in diabetic hemodialysis patients.

hr.quote: During a median follow-up period of 3.8 years, 396 patients in the rosuvastatin group and 408 patients in the placebo group reached the primary end point (9.2 and 9.5 events per 100 patient-years, respectively; hazard ratio for the combined end point in the rosuvastatin group vs. the placebo group, 0.96; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.84 to 1.11; P=0.59).
hr.note: Components (rates per 100 patient-years, rosuvastatin vs placebo): cardiovascular death 7.2 vs 7.3 (P=0.97); nonfatal MI 2.1 vs 2.5 (P=0.23); nonfatal stroke 1.2 vs 1.1 (P=0.42). All-cause death 636 vs 660, HR 0.96 (0.86-1.07), P=0.51. Registry S3: CV deaths 324 vs 324; 'atherosclerotic cardiac event' (nonfatal MI or CHD death) 258 vs 256; coronary/peripheral revascularisation 148 vs 152. Pre-specified subgroups all null. Expected effect if the CTT relationship held (derived, not from a source): 0.79^1.05 ~ 0.78; the planned 19.5% reduction (HR ~0.805) lies below the observed lower CI bound 0.84.

p.note: Methods: 'The score test was used to calculate P values.'

safety_signals.value: Hemorrhagic stroke increased in patients with diabetes: 12 vs 2 events (P=0.03); no effect on overall stroke
safety_signals.quote: there was a marginal increase in hemorrhagic strokes in patients with diabetes who received rosuvastatin (12 events, vs. 2 events in patients with diabetes in the placebo group; P=0.03), which is consistent with the findings of the 4D study.
safety_signals.note: P value corrected from 0.07 to 0.03 by NEJM correction (N Engl J Med 2010;362:1450, doi 10.1056/NEJMx100015, read via Wayback). Diabetic post hoc S11: HR 5.21 (1.17-23.27).

safety_signals.value: No excess muscle events, rhabdomyolysis (3 vs 2), liver disease, cancer or new-onset diabetes
safety_signals.quote: We observed no increase in the incidence of muscle-related adverse events, rhabdomyolysis, or liver disease in the rosuvastatin group as compared with the placebo group. Five cases of rhabdomyolysis were reported during the trial (in two patients receiving placebo and in three patients receiving rosuvastatin).
safety_signals.note: Same paragraph: 'no increase in the number of new cancer diagnoses was seen in our trial' and 'we did not find an excess of new-onset diabetes.'

safety_signals.value: Adverse events similar: any AE 96.3% vs 96.7%; serious AE 82.1% vs 84.1%
safety_signals.quote: Adverse events were reported in 1338 patients who received rosuvastatin (96.3%) and in 1332 patients who received placebo (96.7%). Serious adverse events were reported in 1140 patients who received rosuvastatin (82.1%) and in 1159 patients who received placebo (84.1%).
safety_signals.location: Results, Adherence to Study Therapy and Adverse Events
safety_signals.note: Registry S3 adverse-event module: serious 1140/1389 vs 1159/1378.

safety_signals.value: High discontinuation: 440 stopped after an adverse event (207 vs 233), 370 for renal transplantation (197 vs 173); mean exposure 2.4 years
safety_signals.quote: In addition, 440 patients (207 who were receiving rosuvastatin and 233 who were receiving placebo) discontinued the study medication after an adverse event, including study end points, and 370 patients (197 who were receiving rosuvastatin and 173 who were receiving placebo) discontinued therapy because of renal transplantation.
safety_signals.note: Execution caveat noted by the authors ('It is possible that the withdrawal rate masks the potential benefit of statin therapy'), but a per-protocol analysis was also null. Tablet counts: 91.7% vs 89.5% taken as intended.

genetics.finding: Mendelian randomization: HMGCR (statin target) LDL-lowering variants protect against cardiovascular events, the same per unit LDL-C as PCSK9 variants
genetics.effect: OR 0.81 (0.72-0.90) per 10 mg/dL lower LDL-C for the HMGCR score
genetics.quote: Variants in PCSK9 and HMGCR were associated with nearly identical protective effects on the risk of cardiovascular events per decrease of 10 mg per deciliter (0.26 mmol per liter) in the LDL cholesterol level: odds ratio for cardiovascular events, 0.81 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.74 to 0.89) for PCSK9 and 0.81 (95% CI, 0.72 to 0.90) for HMGCR.

genetics.finding: 2x2 factorial MR: HMGCR variants lowering LDL-C by 2.9 mg/dL associated with 5.3% lower CHD risk
genetics.quote: whereas the HMGCR group had 2.9 mg/dl lower LDL-C and a similar 5.3% lower risk of CHD (OR: 0.947, 95% CI: 0.909 to 0.986).

genetics.finding: HMGCR variants lower LDL-C and slightly raise type 2 diabetes risk and bodyweight (on-target statin effect)
genetics.effect: rs17238484-G: 0.06 mmol/L lower LDL-C, T2D OR 1.02 (1.00-1.05) per allele
genetics.quote: The increased risk of type 2 diabetes noted with statins is at least partially explained by HMGCR inhibition.

genetics.finding: CTT 2005 (pre-readout benchmark): about one-fifth fewer major vascular events per 1 mmol/L LDL-C reduction
genetics.quote: Statin therapy can safely reduce the 5-year incidence of major coronary events, coronary revascularisation, and stroke by about one fifth per mmol/L reduction in LDL cholesterol, largely irrespective of the initial lipid profile or other presenting characteristics.

genetics.finding: CTT 2010: RR 0.78 per 1 mmol/L LDL-C across all patient types
genetics.quote: similar proportional reductions in major vascular events per 1·0 mmol/L LDL cholesterol reduction were found in all types of patient studied (rate ratio [RR] 0·78, 95% CI 0·76-0·80; p<0·0001)

genetics.finding: EAS consensus: LDL causes ASCVD (atherosclerotic events), proportional to absolute LDL-C reduction
genetics.quote: Consistent evidence from numerous and multiple different types of clinical and genetic studies unequivocally establishes that LDL causes ASCVD.

consensus_explanation.summary: Rosuvastatin cut LDL-C by about 43% (about 1.1 mmol/L) at 3 months, but cardiovascular death, MI and stroke were unchanged in 2,773 hemodialysis patients (HR 0.96, 0.84-1.11, P=0.59; 804 events, so the trial was powered for its assumed 19.5% effect). Experts did not blame LDL causality or the drug. They blamed the population: in maintenance hemodialysis, cardiovascular disease is mostly non-atherosclerotic (sudden cardiac death and heart failure from vascular stiffness and calcification, structural heart disease and arrhythmia), so LDL lowering has little to act on. The investigators, AstraZeneca, the NEJM editorial ('promising but ineffective') and KDIGO 2013, which recommends not starting statins in dialysis patients, all took this view. SHARP's authors added an endpoint argument: more than half the primary events in AURORA and 4D were vascular deaths, with only small benefit, whereas the atherosclerotic components were compatible with CTT. The CTT 2016 meta-analysis found little benefit on dialysis (RR 0.94 per mmol/L) even after allowing for smaller LDL reductions and different outcome definitions. Lesser caveats: high discontinuation and statin drop-in, prevalent statin users excluded, and a post hoc hint of fewer cardiac events in diabetics.

open_questions: Category: population (primary), design_or_endpoint (secondary). Experts agree that the hemodialysis cardiovascular disease process (sudden death, heart failure, calcification) does not respond to LDL lowering (S1, S2, S6, S9, S10, S8). SHARP investigators (S7) framed it partly as an endpoint problem: the LDL-weighted effects on atherosclerotic components were compatible with CTT, but vascular deaths made up most of the primary events. SHARP itself, which had only 2527 hemodialysis patients, found no clear benefit on dialysis (see the sharp case), and CTT 2016 found little benefit on dialysis even after adjusting for outcome definitions, so population stays primary. effect_too_small does not fit: the 804 events met the revised 805-event target, and the CI (0.84-1.11) excludes the planned 19.5% reduction.

Placebo-adjusted lipid changes (-41% LDL-C, -1.05 mmol/L) are derived from per-arm 3-month values; the time-averaged LDL-C difference over follow-up was smaller (convergence from drop-outs and statin drop-in) but was NOT FOUND as a number (Figure 1A not read).

On-treatment apoB and non-HDL-C: NOT FOUND (tertiary endpoints in S4; not in S1 text). S1 Tables 1-3 (images) not read, so the counts behind component rates and the baseline hsCRP value are unverified; baseline hsCRP 5.0 mg/L comes from ambiguous Discussion wording.
Randomized counts differ: 2776 (S1, S3), 2775 (S5 baseline paper), 2773 ITT (S1); registry denominators 1389/1384 vs S1 1391/1385.

Design changed mid-trial (2005, after 4D): stroke effect assumed 0%, assumed reduction lowered from 25% to 19.5%, power from 90% to 87%, events from 620 to 805. The primary endpoint itself was not changed.

Authors' own caveats: prevalent statin users (an estimated 35-40% of ESRD patients) were excluded, the event rate was lower than predicted, and discontinuation was high (440 after AEs, 370 for transplant). A post hoc diabetic analysis (S11) found 32% fewer cardiac events (HR 0.68), hypothesis-generating only.
